newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Valeo stays French after sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Valeo stays French after sale.

text.p: French holding company CGIP said on Tuesday it was buying 20 percent of car parts manufacturer Valeo to become the lead shareholder in a group France's car makers have fought to keep in French hands.

Cerus, a holding company owned by Italian financier Carlo de Benedetti, sold the 20 percent stake to Compagnie Generale d'Industrie et de Participations (CGIP), which previously held a stake in Valeo but sold it in 1993.
Other CGIP investments include interests in the industrial and information technology sectors.

Cerus is also selling 3.6 percent to French state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignation (CDC) and another 3.6 percent to U.S. investment fund JP Morgan GT Corp for a total of at least 6.5 billion francs ($1.3 billion).
CDC's purchase will push its stake in Valeo to 5.4 percent from 1.9 percent.

French car industry analysts said the deal was good news for all involved. Valeo had a solid partner in CGIP to develop on its own, even if this would not rule out a merger with another car parts firm in several years as the industry changed.
"Today, they are of a critical size but maybe in three or four years, they could benefit from economies of scale in a merger," said one French auto industry analyst.
"This doesn't mean they won't merge with a U.S. partner eventually," the analyst said.
The French government and carmakers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen were also likely to welcome CGIP's acquisition since they had all been seeking ways to ensure Valeo stayed out of foreign hands.

De Benedetti first made it known more than a year ago he was looking to sell his Valeo stake when he was seeking fresh finances for the Italian computer group Olivetti, from which he has since resigned as chairman.

When news that his Cerus holding company was ready to sell, French car industry circles became worried amid reports of interest from U.S. giants Delphi Automotive Systems, which belongs to General Motors, and TRW Inc.

But threats of a boycott by the French car manufacturers, which are Valeo's biggest clients, is thought to have discouraged any foreign bids. Among the most vociferous supporters of keeping Valeo French was PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet.

In the CGIP deal, Valeo, Europe's second largest car parts maker and a leading supplier of French and German carmakers, said they would also make an advance 1996 dividend downpayment of 10 francs for which Cerus would still be the beneficiary.
In addition, another payout of 10 francs per share would be made to Cerus if Valeo's 1997 net attributable profit is at least equal to 1.45 billion francs, a Cerus statement said.
Cerus said it would use the proceeds partly to pay off debts and would continue to divest financial and property assets while taking controlling stakes in industrial and services groups.

The sale of its stake at 330 francs per share would raise 6.3 billion francs, and the dividend downpayment would generate a further 0.2 billion. The conditional dividends tied to Valeo's 1997 profits would generate another 0.2 billion, Cerus said.

Shares in CGIP opened 5.4-percent higher in Paris and were up 3.76 percent at 1,188 francs at 1114 GMT. Valeo opened 5.05-percent lower but crept back to 301.0 francs, down 3.15 percent. Cerus shares were down 3.43 percent at 132.4 francs.
Analysts said the Valeo slide was probably due to selling by speculators who had still hoped the CGIP deal would fall through and an offer from TRW or another U.S. firm would emerge.
CGIP recently said it raised about 3.2 billion francs from selling its interest in U.S. company Crown Cork and Seal Inc to help pay for the Valeo stake.
